Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) is the top consideration given its abrupt onset, complete painlessness, and profound visual loss—often described as a 'curtain coming down'—and carries time-sensitive implications for potential interventions (e.g., ocular massage, IOP-lowering agents). Non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION) is highly plausible: typically painless, unilateral, and acute, though often with altitudinal or inferior field loss rather than total blindness; however, severe cases can mimic CRAO. Retinal migraine is included due to its transient, painless, monocular nature and association with visual aura during TV viewing (a common trigger), though duration <30 minutes would be more typical—still possible at onset. Optic neuritis is less likely because it is usually painful with eye movement (absent here) and often associated with demyelinating disease, but painless variants occur (~10–20% of cases), warranting inclusion. Branch retinal artery occlusion (BRAO) is considered because it can cause sectoral or profound vision loss depending on involvement; while often partial, extensive BRAO or involvement of the macular branch may present as near-total loss. Conditions like giant cell arteritis are excluded from top 5 due to age context not provided and typical association with pain, jaw claudication, or systemic symptoms—though urgent ESR/CRP would still be indicated if >50 years old. Stroke (posterior circulation) is unlikely given strict monocular involvement—cortical visual loss is always bilateral (homonymous)."}
